The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) seeks to underscore the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024).

In this context, the Anthropocene epoch represents a critical juncture in the Earth's geological history, marking a point of irreversible transformation (Moore, 2016). The neologism 'Anthropocene' has been widely adopted by scholars (Nixon, 2011) to describe the profound effects of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, including climate change (IPCC, 2013), deforestation (WWF, 2020), and habitat destruction (IUCN, 2020). The Anthropocene epoch serves as a poignant reminder of the need for sustainable practices and environmental stewardship (Haraway, 2016), as the Anthropos continues to exert a profound impact on the Earth's biophysical systems.

Furthermore, the introduction of the Anthropocene epoch has sparked a renewed interest in the study of human-environment interactions (Barnosky et al., 2011), highlighting the complex relationships between human societies and the natural environment (Nixon, 2011). This interdisciplinary approach (Smith & Zeder, 2013) seeks to understand the intricate dynamics of human activities and their effects on the Earth's biophysical systems, ultimately informing strategies for mitigating the impacts of anthropogenic activities (Witze, 2024).

In conclusion, the Anthropocene epoch represents a significant milestone in the Earth's geological history, marking a point of irreversible transformation precipitated by human activities. The neologism 'Anthropocene' has been widely adopted by scholars to describe the profound effects of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, and the introduction of the Anthropocene epoch serves as a poignant reminder of the need for sustainable practices and environmental stewardship.
